faqs.q: A raccoon got into my Marion attic. What happens to it?
faqs.a: Relocation is the one outcome we will not sell you: SCDNR is explicit that routine relocation is against state law, and the 100-yard rule in state code says a captured animal must be destroyed or relocated only with a department permit. Our Marion approach is eviction first — the raccoon exits through a one-way door and cannot re-enter — backed by removal under a depredation permit when eviction is not enough, plus full sealing. Raccoons are also the state's leading rabies species in Department of Public Health testing, which is why attic cleanup is part of the visit.

faqs.q: We keep finding snakes around our Marion house. What can be done?
faqs.a: Start with identification, not panic. Around Marion, the everyday snakes are non-venomous rat snakes and racers; the caution species are the copperhead, which is statewide, and the cottonmouth around wet ground, swamp edges, and pond banks. Keep distance, bring pets in, and tell us the size, pattern, and where it sheltered. We identify from photos or on site, handle non-listed snakes where appropriate, and treat venomous encounters as safety work. Reducing cover and rodent food near the foundation lowers repeat sightings more than any single capture.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Marion actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around historic district and Catfish Creek neighborhoods of the county seat: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

Mullins.wildlife_intro:
Mullins keeps our crew busy around the tobacco-market town streets and farm roads north of Marion. Two problems account for most visits: gray squirrels in town canopy streets, and skunks denning at outbuildings.

Early-1900s farm-town housing, tobacco-era homes, and postwar ranches sit on crawlspaces above soil that stays damp much of the year. Flat, wet ground after summer storms pushes snakes and burrowing animals onto higher, drier lots — frequently the lots with houses on them — which is when many of our calls here start.

Removal without repair does not hold in Mullins, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Nichols crawlspace. What happens next?
faqs.a: In Nichols, opossums move into crawlspaces through broken vents and loose doors, then rotate dens every few days, which is why sightings come and go. We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

faqs.q: Pigeons and starlings are nesting in my Nichols vents. Can they be removed?
faqs.a: Pigeons, European starlings, and house sparrows are the birds we can work on in Nichols — vents screened, nests cleared, and spikes or netting fitted so the birds move on. Native birds are different: woodpeckers, chimney swifts, and nesting songbirds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so those jobs are deterrence and timing, waiting out the nest and sealing after the young fledge. Around Little Pee Dee swamp farms in the county's east, vent and soffit nests are the calls we see most.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Nichols home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Nichols that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Nichols.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Nichols and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Little Pee Dee swamp farms in the county's east. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in sandy field-edge yards, then about bats in tobacco-barn and gable roosts.

Housing here runs from historic in-town streets to farm roads, and most of it predates modern sealed construction — open vents and pier foundations are the norm. Blackwater rivers and swamp drains thread this farm country, and wildlife follows them: raccoons, opossums, and armadillos work the wet edges, then den in the nearest barn, porch, or crawlspace.

Before we leave a Nichols home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Sellers attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In Sellers we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near Great Pee Dee-side farm country in the county's west, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Sellers house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Sellers job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near Great Pee Dee-side farm country in the county's west with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.
